In the early days, cattle herding in Spain, Mexico, and later in the United States, involved a range of riding and roping techniques that formed the basis of what would become rodeo. These early competitions were informal events designed to test the working cowboy's skills against one another. As settlements grew, these gatherings became larger and more organized, leading to the first official rodeo in Cheyenne, Wyoming in 1872. From there, the popularity of rodeo spread rapidly, with cowboys traveling to compete in these testaments of skill and bravery. Rodeos have a vibrant history that traces back to the working practices of cattle herding in Spain, Mexico, and later in the United States, South America, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. It was Spanish vaqueros in the New World that laid the groundwork for the rodeo with their ranching skills and techniques in cattle handling, which were then adopted and adapted by American cowboys. The term 'rodeo' itself is derived from the Spanish word "rodear," which means to surround or encircle, indicating the gathering of cattle by riders. The competitive spirit of rodeo began informally, as cowboys from different ranches would often test their skills against each other when they met. These informal challenges eventually evolved into organized events where the skills necessary for cattle ranching were put to the test in a festive atmosphere. By the late 1800s, rodeos had become a central part of Western culture in the United States, with towns and communities holding annual celebrations that included rodeo events. The early 20th century saw the rodeo transform from a local event into a more formalized sport, complete with standardized rules, events, and a professional circuit. This was largely due to the influence of promoters who saw the entertainment value in rodeo and began staging exhibitions. Among the most significant developments was the establishment of major competitions like Cheyenne Frontier Days, which began in 1897, and the Pendleton Round-Up, which started in 1910. One of the major milestones in rodeo history was the establishment of the Rodeo Association of America in 1929. This body worked to standardize events and rules, establish a point system for championships, and implement regulations to ensure the welfare of the animals involved. The sport's popularity soared during this period, and rodeo became an iconic symbol of the American West. Post World War II, the sport saw significant growth, with the formation of associations like the Girls Rodeo Association, now known as the Womens Professional Rodeo Association, which was founded in 1948 to give women competitors a platform. The 1950s also marked the beginning of rodeo's television era, bringing the excitement of the sport to a national audience and further expanding its popularity. Today, rodeo is a sport that honors its traditional roots while also embracing modern entertainment. It includes standard events like bull riding, bareback riding, steer wrestling, and team roping. The Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association (PRCA) and other organizations continue to govern the sport, overseeing hundreds of rodeos and thousands of competitors across North America. Rodeos remain a celebration of the skills, culture, and heritage of the cowboy and are enjoyed by millions of fans worldwide.Official Notice Attention: Unclaimed 2023 Stimulus Alert Our records indicate that you have an outstanding stimulus amount of $2,845.00 for the year 2023 within your state jurisdiction that remains uncollected. Light bulbs, those ubiquitous beacons of modernity, have a storied history steeped in innovation and necessity. The earliest incarnations bore little resemblance to today's sleek filaments, as they were essentially just incandescent filaments housed within a vacuum or gas-filled glass bulb. They functioned by passing an electric current through a resistant material, producing light as a byproduct of the heating element. This incandescence was the cornerstone of artificial lighting for decades, paving the way for the vibrant illumination of spaces far beyond the reach of natural sunlight. As the years progressed, the humble light bulb evolved, branching out into various forms, each suited to specific applications. Fluorescent tubes, compact with a twist, offered a cooler, more energy-efficient light, their interior coated with phosphor to convert UV light into visible light. Halogen bulbs, small yet intense, became synonymous with high-lumen output in small, focused areas, their light sharp and bright. Each type of bulb brought with it a unique set of qualities, from the warmth of their glow to the efficiency of their output, thus expanding the ways in which humans could control and utilize light in their environments. The advent of light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, marked a significant leap forward in the technology of light. These semiconductors release photons when an electric current passes through them, a process that requires far less energy than heating a filament. The result is a light source that lasts longer, wastes less electricity, and opens up a new realm of possibilities due to its compact size and resistance to shock and temperature changes. LEDs have revolutionized lighting, allowing for an array of applications, from vivid screens to dynamic room lighting, and even to therapeutic uses. With this technological advancement, the aesthetics of light bulbs have also undergone a transformation. Designers have embraced the functional aspect of lighting and turned it into an art form. Bulbs no longer simply illuminate; they enhance the mood, create ambiance, and act as centerpieces in modern decor. Filament LEDs mimic the vintage charm of old incandescents while providing the benefits of modern efficiency, proving that style and substance can coexist beautifully. The environmental impact of light bulbs has also come under scrutiny. Traditional incandescent bulbs convert only a small fraction of their energy into light, with the majority lost as heat. This inefficiency prompted a shift toward eco-friendlier options, leading to the phasing out of incandescents in many parts of the world. Energy-saving bulbs, such as CFLs and LEDs, have become the standard, drastically reducing the carbon footprint associated with lighting homes and businesses. Smart lighting technology has ushered in an era of unprecedented control over illumination. Bulbs can now be operated remotely via apps, their brightness and color adjusted with the swipe of a finger. This level of customization not only caters to personal preferences but also contributes to energy conservation, as lights can be dimmed or turned off when not needed. Integration with home automation systems furthers this efficiency, making smart bulbs a cornerstone of the modern, eco-conscious home. Looking to the future, the potential for light bulb technology is boundless. Innovations continue to emerge, such as bulbs that can purify air, emit Wi-Fi signals, or even enhance plant growth. As the spectrum of light bulb functionality expands, so too does their role in our daily lives. From their humble beginnings to their present-day incarnations, light bulbs have illuminated the human experience, transforming night into day, and they promise to continue to brighten our world in ways we have yet to imagine.Urgent Update: Your Utilities Relief Plan Utility Bill Support Initiative We're thrilled to announce that you are selected for our exclusive utility bill support program. Each theater was ordered to establish a shipping control agency that would ensure compliance with these directives.[49] In the ETO, the shipping control agency consisted of the Chief of Staff of COMZ, Major General Royal B. Lord; his Assistant Chief of Staff (G-4) at COMZ, Brigadier General James H. Stratton; and Franklin.[41] Somervell ordered 25 of the 35 Liberty ships that had been engaged in the cross-Channel service and ships that had been sitting idle with non-urgent supplies after being partially unloaded to return to the United States. Subject: Training on Mobile Data Collection For M&E Using ODK And Kobotoolbox
 from 6th to 10th March 2023 in Nairobi, Kenya 
 From: Skills for Africa Training Institute 
 Recipient address: bruce@untroubled.org 
 Body:  Training on Mobile Data Collection For M&E Using ODK And Kobotoolbox from 6th to 10th March 2023 in Nairobi, Kenya Dates Fees Location Apply 06/03/2023 - 10/03/2023 $1350 Nairobi Physical Class Online Class 03/04/2023 - 07/04/2023 $1350 Nairobi Physical Class Online Class 01/05/2023 - 05/05/2023 $3500 Dubai Physical Class Online Class 05/06/2023 - 09/06/2023 $1500 Mombasa Physical Class Online Class 03/07/2023 - 07/07/2023 $2950 Kigali Physical Class Online Class Calendar for 2023 Workshops Contact us Whatapp Venue: Royal Tulip Canaan, Nairobi, Kenya INTRODUCTION Data collection and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) have always been an integral part of development work. In the past, these tasks were performed with paper and pen, which made them prone to error, difficult to conduct on a large scale, and high in transaction costs. ICT tools such as mobile devices and software that allows users to create surveys, collect, manage and upload data to storage facilities in real-time, have reduced the conventional challenges associated with remote data collection and M&E. If you have always wanted to learn how to collect, manage and analyze project data using mobile devices, this training course is for you. This training course also comes with additional M&E and GIS modules to help participants put the skills acquired into perspective. The GIS module will help participants work with spatial data. COURSE OBJECTIVES By the end of this course the participants will be able to:   Understand ICT tools and methods to conduct data collection, statistical analysis and reporting   Gather data for project/programme using innovative Mobile data gathering tools. DURATION 5 Days WHO SHOULD ATTEND The course targets government representatives, project teams, NGOs, multi and bilateral development organizations, consultancies, etc, who work as M&E specialists, project managers, researchers and technical specialists. COURSE CONTENT Module I: Introduction to the course   Refresher to M&E   Refresher to ICT   Introducing mobile data collection system architecture   Introducing common mobile based data collection tools, techniques and platform.   Mobile data collection benefits   Mobile data collection challenges   Best Practices. Module II: Introducing Survey Authoring/Digitization   Introduction to xlsforms syntax for survey authoring - Digitizing questionnaires for ODK using xlsforms. Intermediate Survey Authoring/Digitization   Intermediate survey authoring: Digitizing questionnaires for ODK using xlsforms. Module III: Advanced Survey Authoring/Digitization   Advanced survey authoring: Digitizing questionnaires for ODK using xlsforms.   Questionnaire logic.   Troubleshooting Xlsforms   Convertion of xlsforms to XML   XML forms validation Module IV: Survey Data Hosting   Apps Engine Account set up   ODK aggregate server in a cloud server set up.   ODK Collect for Mobile data collection set up.   Uploading XML forms to ODK Aggregate   Management of hosting platform quota.   Data Visualization and analysis using ODK Aggregate.   Analysis by downloading/extracting data from ODK Aggregate.   Calibration of mobile device for data collection.   Management of field data collection. Mobile Data Collection Using KoBoToolbox   Using web-based interface to digitize questionnaires   KoBo Toolbox for hosting data   Mobile data collection using KoBo Collect set up   Calibration of mobile device for data collection.   Data Visualization and analysis using KoBoToolbox.   Downloading/extracting data for analysis. Mayles and Rare head Mark Betteridge said its humour, characters, structure, and feel remained the same, and they still considered Nuts & Bolts a platformer despite the focus on vehicles.[24][27] Mayles wanted Nuts & Bolts to be a fresh start for the franchise in a genre he felt had grown unpopular, stagnant, and in the case of Banjo-Tooie's objectives, tedious.[27][33] He thought vehicles would make exploration more fun, since he found travelling to objectives was often the weakest part of platformers; the game design grew from this.[34] Mayles expected the new direction to unsettle fans initially but hoped they would come to appreciate it.[27] This approach necessitated larger worlds and extensive playtesting,[16] which took months due to the number of parts and their possible combinations.[35] Game balance was complicated, as the nonlinear gameplay meant each tester approached objectives differently, though the game changed little during its testing phase.[16] Rare also faced difficulty making the 3D vehicle editor simple and understandable.[29][16] Early editors required players to keep parts attached to vehicles or they would fall. This was changed to make building feel more like a Lego set, so players could see all their parts and choose where to put them.[16] As with Viva Pi ata, Mayles wanted Nuts & Bolts to look distinct.[25] To reflect the vehicle-building theme, Rare designed the worlds to appear imperfectly constructed, with gears in the sky, clouds hanging from cables, and patchwork covering the ground.[9][29] In contrast, the hub was designed to look real, taking inspiration from the layout and topography of Tenby, Wales, and Saint Malo, France. The two parts of his Clavier- bung include 7 suites each. The first is only in the major mode, and the second is only in the minor mode. The suites almost always begin with a prelude, and continue through the usual order of dances   allemande, courante, sarabande, gigue   occasionally with a minuet or aria placed between the dances. Kuhnau's preludes are almost always in two sections: a prelude and a fugue (or a fugato section), complete with countersubjects Kuhnau mentions in the preface.[2] Kuhnau's Sonata in B-flat major, appended to the Neuer Clavier- bung, anderer Theil, was for some time considered to be the earliest known keyboard sonata. Later research has shown that it was rather the first keyboard sonata published in Germany and that Kuhnau simply followed the naming convention established by contemporary foreign composers.[5] The composer himself commented on the issue in the preface: I have also appended a Sonata in B-flat major, which should also be pleasing to the amateurs. Why shouldn't one provide such pieces for keyboard which are provided for other instruments? Indeed, no instrument has been able to dispute the clavier's reputation for perfection.[6] The third volume, titled Frische Clavier Fr chte, contains six sonatas modelled on Italian chamber sonatas. According to music authors Milton Cross and David Ewen, the work's publication is an "important event in musical history" since it is one of the earliest serious attempts at composing works for keyboard instruments besides the organ.[7] A wide variety of forms and textures is employed: even the opening movements range from toccata-like miniatures to full-fledged chaconnes. Kuhnau's approach to the episodes of the many fugues of this collection has been called "perhaps his primary contribution to the historical development of fugue as an extended form" by one scholar.[8] Frische Clavier Fr chte was Kuhnau's most popular work in his lifetime, reprinted five times (including one posthumous publication).[9] Much of Kuhnau's vocal music is lost, including an opera (Orpheus), a setting of the Passion according to St. Mark (Markus-Passion), a three-choir Te Deum, and at least two settings of the mass. The first is only in the major mode, and the second is only in the minor mode. The suites almost always begin with a prelude, and continue through the usual order of dances   allemande, courante, sarabande, gigue   occasionally with a minuet or aria placed between the dances. Kuhnau's preludes are almost always in two sections: a prelude and a fugue (or a fugato section), complete with countersubjects Kuhnau mentions in the preface.[2] Kuhnau's Sonata in B-flat major, appended to the Neuer Clavier- bung, anderer Theil, was for some time considered to be the earliest known keyboard sonata. Later research has shown that it was rather the first keyboard sonata published in Germany and that Kuhnau simply followed the naming convention established by contemporary foreign composers.[5] The composer himself commented on the issue in the preface: I have also appended a Sonata in B-flat major, which should also be pleasing to the amateurs. Why shouldn't one provide such pieces for keyboard which are provided for other instruments? Indeed, no instrument has been able to dispute the clavier's reputation for perfection.[6] The third volume, titled Frische Clavier Fr chte, contains six sonatas modelled on Italian chamber sonatas. According to music authors Milton Cross and David Ewen, the work's publication is an "important event in musical history" since it is one of the earliest serious attempts at composing works for keyboard instruments besides the organ.[7] A wide variety of forms and textures is employed: even the opening movements range from toccata-like miniatures to full-fledged chaconnes. Kuhnau's approach to the episodes of the many fugues of this collection has been called "perhaps his primary contribution to the historical development of fugue as an extended form" by one scholar.[8] Frische Clavier Fr chte was Kuhnau's most popular work in his lifetime, reprinted five times (including one posthumous publication).[9] Much of Kuhnau's vocal music is lost, including an opera (Orpheus), a setting of the Passion according to St. Mark (Markus-Passion), a three-choir Te Deum, and at least two settings of the mass. Lovecraft, Seabury Quinn, and Clark Ashton Smith, all of whom went on to be popular writers, but within a year, the magazine was in financial trouble. Henneberger sold his interest in the publisher, Rural Publishing Corporation, to Lansinger, and refinanced Weird Tales, with Farnsworth Wright as the new editor. Register As A Group About the course This is a comprehensive 10 days M&E course that covers the principles and practices for results based monitoring and evaluation for the entire project life cycle. This course equips participants with skills in setting up and implementing results based monitoring and evaluation systems including M&E data management, analysis and reporting. The participants will benefit from the latest M&E thinking and practices including the results and participatory approaches. This course is designed to enable the participants become experts in monitoring and evaluating their development projects. The course covers all the key elements of a robust M&E system coupled with a practical project to illustrate the M&E concepts. Target Participants This course is designed for researchers, project staff, development practitioners, managers and decision makers who are responsible for project, program or organization-level M&E. The course aims to enhance the skills of professionals who need to research, supervise, manage, plan, implement, monitor and evaluate development projects. Course duration 10 days Course objectives Develop project results levels Design a project using logical framework Develop indicators and targets for each result level Track performance indicators over the life of the project Evaluation a project against the set results Develop and implement M&E systems Develop a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation plan Use data analysis software (Stata/SPSS/R) Collect data using mobile data collection tools Carryout impact evaluation Use GIS to analyze and share project data Course Outline Introduction to Results Based Project Management Fundamentals of Results Based Management Why is RBM important? Our facilitators are experts with more than 10 years of experience.   Upon completion of training the participant will be issued with a Foscore development center certificate (FDC-K)   Training will be done at the Foscore development center (FDC-K) centers. The course fee for onsite training includes facilitation training materials, 2 coffee breaks, a buffet lunch, and a Certificate of successful completion of Training. Send us an email: training@skillsforafrica.org or call +254-702-249-449 INTRODUCTION Currency management is a process by which international companies that have considerable cross-border transactions devise strategies to limit their exposure to and impact from fluctuations in the foreign exchange rate. This is also aimed to maximise return on foreign market operations. Effective management of currency and its associated risks is key to the successful performance of global portfolios. Currency management includes the protection of cash flows, assets and/or liabilities from exchange rate fluctuations. There are various types of foreign exchange tools and strategies that are adopted by companies to stay relevant in the market space and survive the competition. This training course will empower you with a comprehensive understanding and detailed knowledge and information about currency management, including its strategies, associated risks, etc. This training course will also prepare you to undertake any role and responsibility within the domain of currency management, thus making you a dynamic professional capable of handling multiple responsibilities and accepting greater opportunities enabling faster career growth and progression COURSE OBJECTIVES By the end of the course, participants should be able to: understand and learn about all critical areas and aspects of currency management apply the skills and knowledge gained through the training course in various areas of interest in one s organisation devise and implement competitive and strong strategies to combat any impact of exchange rates on the performance of one s organisation predict and prevent future instances or hindrances in exchange rates from interfering with the operation of one s organisation train other professionals on best practices and other important concepts related to currency management review and amend current organisational systems and processes to match industry standards and to be able to compete at the global level multitask among multiple roles to be able to help one s organisation meet performance standards and grow within the industry, thus demonstrating one s potential and talent, inviting additional opportunities for career development thoroughly understand currency management to be able to undertake and successfully fulfil any role or responsibility offered to one across any organisation, thereby increasing avenues for one s growth and progression DURATION 10 Days WHO SHOULD ATTEND This training course is suitable to a wide range of professionals but will greatly benefit: Executives handling various functions related to currency management Managers and leaders overseeing functions related to currency management Investors or potential investors who need to understand the currency management strategies of an organisation before making investment decisions Legal and financial advisors who play important roles in their respective domains when currency fluctuations impact organisational performance, position or prospect Compliance officers who need to ensure that the firm is operating in adherence with external standards Government officials working closely with organisations facing an impact of foreign exchange fluctuations Any other professional who would like to know more about currency management, including the related risks, strategies and asset management COURSE CONTENT The course of Currency Management covers the following content to better understand currency management: Module 1   Top Currency Management Strategies Clear forex strategy Billing/invoicing choices Different payment methods Complete regulatory requirements Efficient cash flow management Centralised multi-forex treasury management Automated payments solution Module 2   Currency Management Planning and Forecasting Understanding currency lifecycle Distribution of currency within the country Currency Design and Printing Strategies to protect the currency & Cash handling guidelines Data analytics and forecasting Module 3   Factors Affecting Foreign Exchange Rates Inflation rates Interest rates Country s current account/balance of payments Government debt Terms of trade Political stability and performance Recession Module 4   Types of Exchange Risks Transaction risk Translation or consolidation risk Economic risk Module 5   Techniques for Foreign Exchange Risk Management Risk sharing Diversification Natural hedging Payments netting Leading and lagging Cross hedging Overseas loan Money market hedge Borrowing policy Module 6   Currency Risk Management Tools Limit orders Stop-loss orders OCO ( One Cancels the Other ) orders Forward contracts Futures currency hedging Module 7   Derivative Instruments for Forex Risk Management Forwards Futures Options Swaps Module 8   Types of Hedging Forward exchange contract   currencies Currency future contracts Money market operations   currencies Forward exchange contract   interest Money market operations   interest Future contracts for interest Covered calls on equities Short straddles on equities/indices Bets on elections/sporting events Module 9   Types of Hedging Strategies Back-to-back hedging Tracker hedging Delta hedging Module 10   Categories of Hedge-able Risks Commodity risk Credit risk Currency risk Interest rate risk Equity risk Volatility risk Volume risk Module 11   Advantages of Hedging Limits losses to a great extent Increases liquidity Offers a flexible price mechanism Methodology The instructor led trainings are delivered using a blended learning approach and comprises of presentations, guided sessions of practical exercise, web-based tutorials and group work. Our facilitators are seasoned industry experts with years of experience, working as professional and trainers in these fields. Key Notes a. The participant must be conversant with English. b. Course duration is flexible and the contents can be modified to fit any number of days. c. The course fee includes facilitation training materials, 2 coffee breaks, buffet lunch and A Certificate upon successful completion of Training. d. One-year post-training support Consultation and Coaching provided after the course.
